extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, judge advocates, and military personnel administrators
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of legal standards and interpretive rulings governing military rank, relative and brevet rank, suspension and its effects, use of the Red Cross emblem, domicile/residence rules for service members, and retirement/retiring-board procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative rank of volunteer officers determined by muster-in/appointment date
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative rank of volunteer officers mustered into the service under the provisions of April 22, 1898 (30 Stat. 361), dates from the date of appointment; relative rank must be determined by reference to the time of muster-in and not from the time of enrollment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites opinions holding that the date of appointment/muster-in, not enrollment, fixes relative rank for volunteers (see 23 Op. Atty. Gen., 406 and related citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified nonstandard positions given statutory relative rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain appointed positions (e.g., master of the sword at the United States Military Academy) are 'officers' and, under statute, are given a specified 'relative rank' (e.g., of a captain, mounted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such positions as officers for purposes of rank when a statute grants them a relative rank; see act of March 3, 1905 (33 Stat. 850) and cited opinion C. 18009, Mar. 23, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncommissioned cadet service does not count for later relative rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Naval cadets who were not commissioned officers cannot, upon afterwards becoming lieutenants in the Army, compute for relative rank their period of service as such cadets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding referenced (P. 25,214, June, 1888) treats uncommissioned cadet time as non-creditable for later relative-rank computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers placed on a single list per arm according to rank to determine advancement rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statutes cited (section 2 of act of June 18, 1878 and act of Oct. 1, 1890), all officers of each arm of the service are placed upon one list in accordance with their rank in the several grades; this list represents their lineal or military rank and serves to determine rights in respect of advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the consolidated list order (files) to determine promotions and precedence among officers of an arm; legal citations and examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting 'reduced X files in military rank'
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence 'to be reduced thirty files in military rank' means a loss of thirty files in lineal military rank; i.e., the officer's name will be reduced thirty files in the list of officers of his grade in his arm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an interpretive rule for penal sentences affecting an officer's position on the list (citations G. 12440, Apr. 30, 1902; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive relief limited; Congress is source of general relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority of the executive department to grant relief is limited by strict law and to a few subjects; Congress, as the fountain of general relief, by authorizing special appointments and disposing of public money, can adequately provide for nearly all applications for relief which the Executive is not empowered to grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides expectations about remedies and who has power to provide relief to officers/soldiers; background principle used to interpret relief requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevet rank only as incident to full lower-grade rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevet rank can properly neither be conferred nor take effect except as an incident to full rank of a lower grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited holdings (R. 21, 608, Aug., 1866; C. 2122, Mar. 10, 1896; 12419, Apr. 14, 1902) emphasize brevet cannot exist independently of an underlying full rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment to duty under brevet rank is limited in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 1211, R.S., an officer may be assigned to duty according to his brevet rank for a special command or duty, and such assignment will not be effective generally but only for the purposes of such command or duty and during its continuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: officer assigned 'while in command of' a department may exercise privileges of brevet rank only during that command (R. 42,21, Oct., 1878).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevet rank while assigned becomes actual rank for assignment period
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer has been duly assigned to duty or command according to a certain brevet rank, that rank becomes his actual military rank for the period of the assignment: he may exercise the authority of such rank, wear the uniform, and be addressed by the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effects include wearing uniform and exercising authority; some privileges (e.g., aids-de-camp of a general) may require additional authorization (Secretary of War).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension from rank does not alter list position or office
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension from rank does not deprive the officer of the right to rise in files in his grade (for example upon promotion of the senior officer); the number of an officer in the list of his grade is incident to his appointment to office as conferred, and suspension does not affect the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of files is a continuing punishment; treating suspension as loss of files would extend punishment indefinitely after suspension term—contrary to military law principles (R. 33, 69, 109, June, 1872).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effects of suspension: loss of minor rights of precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of a suspension from rank is that the officer loses for the time the minor rights and privileges of priority and precedence annexed to rank or command (e.g., right to select quarters); but suspension alone cannot deprive him of quarters previously duly selected and occupied at time of suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspended officer still entitled to some quarters assigned by commander; military authorities have addressed this and reaffirmed the rule (Secretary of War decision May 27, 1876; War Dept. 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension resulting from failed promotion examination dates from accrual of promotion right
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer fails in his examination for promotion under the act of October 1, 1890, with resultant suspension from rank for one year, the suspension will date from the date when the right to promotion accrued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how to compute start of suspension when tied to promotion examination result (C. 29327, Dec. 19, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Red Cross/Geneva emblem has international value only by treaty
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of international law the emblem of the Red Cross has no value or meaning except that which has been placed upon it by treaty (Geneva Convention); its international protection exists only between acceding nations and under the Convention's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the Geneva Convention adopted the emblem for ameliorating the wounded of armies and limits who may use it and when (C. 16453, June 7, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sanitary formations may use emblem only with home government consent and belligerent acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil sanitary formations of a neutral nation may, with the consent of their own government, offer services to a belligerent power and, if accepted by that belligerent, assist in caring for the sick and wounded; only with consent and acceptance do they become part of that belligerent's sanitary establishment and receive protection under the Geneva emblem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a civil organization enters a belligerent area without the required consent/acceptance, it is not entitled to Geneva Convention protection (example: American Red Cross entry into Mexico 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal law governs misuse of the Red Cross emblem within US peace jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the American National Red Cross charter, use of the Red Cross emblem under certain circumstances and for certain purposes is forbidden and made a misdemeanor in federal court; misuse in the presence of US military in peace is addressed as a civilian misdemeanor, with military duty limited to lodging information with civil authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In war, however, the federal government must ensure conformity to Geneva requirements for aid societies operating with US armies (Art.10, Geneva Convention 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: False representation as Red Cross agent is misdemeanor in US
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the jurisdiction of the United States it is a misdemeanor for a person to falsely represent himself as a member of or an agent for the American National Red Cross to solicit money or material, or to wear the Red Cross or an imitation for fraudulent purposes (36 Stat. 604).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military authorities have no right to arrest such a misdemeanant but should lodge information with civilian law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domicile of service member is that at appointment/entry and not changed by being stationed elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer's domicile during continuance in service is the domicile or residence which he had when he received his appointment or entered into enlistment; this residence does not change while the officer remains in military service as movements are due to military orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: voting rights remain at legal residence; liability to taxation as resident of original locality generally unaffected; case citations and authority provided (C. 12028, Apr. 28, 1911; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary absence in service does not destroy prior legal residence absent clear intent to change
rubrics_metrics.description: If a legal residence in a certain State has once existed, mere temporary absence, however long continued as the result of enlistment, will not destroy it; animus revertendi to original domicile is presumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations (R. 50, 392, June, 1886; others) and examples illustrating that absence under orders does not create a new legal residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: To establish new domicile while in service requires clear, convincing acts showing intent
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer cannot make a place his residence merely by declaration; he must take definite action indicating intention and ability to permanently remain (e.g., acquiring a dwelling, moving family, entering into business) to constitute legal residence or domicile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because officers are subject to orders, evidence of intent must be strong; less evidence needed for officers with stable postings (chiefs of staff corps, retired officers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minors' residence rules: unemancipated vs emancipated
rubrics_metrics.description: An unemancipated minor cannot acquire a residence different from that of his father; an emancipated minor can acquire a bona fide actual residence different from that of his father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited holdings (C. 1220, Apr., 1895; C. 6615, June 17, 1899) clarify residence acquisition rules for minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary retirement eligibility: service-length thresholds and counting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary retirement for officers is provided for at 30 years' service (with specified counting rules) and 40 years' service; whether certain service (e.g., United States Military Academy or midshipman service) counts is addressed in detailed subrules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synopsis lists points: date of retirement, count of service including USMA, and that midshipman service may not count in certain contexts; see full retirement synopsis for statutory references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary retirement (retiring board) standards and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Retiring boards consider acquired disability and reasons for retirement; they cannot retire an officer for 'moral obliquity' or future contingent incapacity; jurisdiction of the board is not limited as to time and rules govern taking depositions, charge non-trialability, presence of officer, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules include duties of members and recorder, allowance of minority reports, and the board's practical operations (see retiring-board procedure references and page citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and evidentiary rules for retiring-board findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Important definitions for board findings include: 'active service', 'permanent' (test: is disease durable?), 'incident of the service' or 'line of duty'; if no evidence to contrary, 'line of duty' is presumed; for 'not line of duty' the reasonable doubt rule applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions guide whether disability is compensable/retirable; the synopsis outlines tests and evidentiary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's role and limits on action following retiring-board findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's action: a retiring-board finding is a recommendation only; disapproval effects no change in status; President has discretion in certain cases (e.g., 'not line of duty'); one Presidential action exhausts the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains executive oversight and limits on re-evaluation after decision; see cited procedural summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining boards (act of Oct. 1, 1890) are not courts for trying moral delinquency; officers entitled to full hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: An examining board under the act is not a court for trial of moral delinquency; the officer is nevertheless entitled to a full hearing on issues of moral delinquency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes disciplinary trial processes from medical/examining board proceedings; procedural consequences for capacity findings are described (multiple scenarios for first/second examinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retirement order finality and retired-officer status rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Retirement order cannot be revoked; retired officers have specific status rules concerning uniform/title, may be in military service for some statutory purposes, may be subject to general court-martial, may hold civil office subject to limits, and have specified pay/mileage/transportation rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The synopsis enumerates detailed subrules on rights and restrictions of retired officers (active duty recall, employment, burial, pay, mileage, transport to home, and ineligibilities).
